Overview # Hello fellow expats and friends preparing to take their first steps into Germany! During our adventure of building a new life in Germany, we set out on a long family journey packed with our belongings: driving from Istanbul to Munich. This post serves as a guide for anyone considering this exact experience—hitting the road with two small kids, an LPG-powered car, and countless bags. If you are torn between flying and driving, or looking for practical solutions while moving to Germany, this detailed story of our experience is just for you.
Moving to Germany, especially coming from Turkey, brings along many logistical challenges. Transporting belongings, maintaining family routines, and travel comfort—especially for families with children—are some of the most critical aspects of this process. Keeping these factors in mind, we decided to drive our own car instead of dealing with airline baggage limits, layovers, and airport stress with young children. This decision offered a much more enjoyable and controllable travel experience than we ever expected.
So, when does this route make sense for you? If you, like us, are traveling with two young children, plan to carry lots of belongings, perhaps even furniture, bicycles, or pets, want a flexible travel schedule, and would love to see different sides of Europe, this guide will inspire you. Setting out in your own car can be budget-friendly and gives you the freedom to move at your own pace, stopping whenever and wherever you want.
What should motivate you to read this post? You will find everything here, from the border crossing procedures you might encounter while relocating to Germany, to the vignette (toll sticker) systems on European motorways, smart tactics for long-distance driving with kids, and even the camaraderie of Turkish truck drivers you meet along the way. I’ll share all the practical insights, experiences, and tips we gathered to make your journey less stressful, more affordable, and truly memorable. Fasten your seatbelts, let’s hit the road!
Step-by-Step Process # This roughly 1,500-kilometer journey from Istanbul to Munich requires navigating different countries, diverse road conditions, and varied experiences. Here is our step-by-step route and what you need to know:
Step 1: Istanbul – Bulgarian Border (Kapıkule/Hamzabeyli) # Where: Leaving Istanbul via the E80 motorway towards Edirne. How: Exit through Kapıkule or Hamzabeyli border crossings on the Turkish side, and enter through Kapitan Andreevo or Lesovo on the Bulgarian side. Kapıkule is busier; Hamzabeyli can be much calmer. How Long It Takes: About 2–3 hours from Istanbul to Kapıkule. Border wait times can range from 1 hour to 4–5 hours depending on congestion. It is generally calmer late at night or on weekdays. Things to Watch Out For: Make sure your passports are valid and your Schengen visa is multiple-entry and currently valid. Keep your vehicle registration document and Green Card (international motor insurance certificate) handy. For detailed info on the Green Card: Green Card Insurance Guide. Online / In-Person: Border crossings involve purely in-person passport and customs checks. No prior appointment is needed. Step 2: Across Bulgaria (Kapitan Andreevo – Sofia – Calafat Border) # Where: After Kapitan Andreevo, take the A4 motorway to Sofia, then head towards the Vidin/Calafat border via the A2. However, our route went west from Sofia through a mountainous area directly towards the Calafat border crossing. How: Once you enter Bulgaria, purchasing a vignette (toll sticker) is mandatory. You can buy one at kiosks right after the border or at the first gas stations. Options typically include 1 week, 1 month, or 1 year. Bulgarian motorways are generally in decent shape. However, part of the road from Sofia towards Romania’s Calafat border (heading to Vidin) is mountainous, winding, and not a divided highway. How Long It Takes: 3–4 hours from Kapitan Andreevo to Sofia, and 3–4 hours from Sofia to Calafat (including the mountain section). Crossing Bulgaria altogether takes roughly 6–8 hours. Things to Watch Out For: The mountain pass between Sofia and Calafat can be exhausting due to narrow, winding roads. We drove it at night with low visibility, which made it even more tiring. If possible, try driving this part in daylight—both for safety and the scenic views. Watch speed limits strictly in Bulgaria; speed traps are common. Online / In-Person: The vignette can be purchased physically or online (bgtoll.bg). The border crossing is handled in-person over the New Europe Bridge (Calafat–Vidin Bridge), which requires a toll. Step 3: Across Romania (Calafat – A1 Motorway – Nădlac/Arad Border) # Where: After entering Romania at Calafat, head north along the E79 route towards Pitești, then join the A1 motorway heading towards Budapest. How: You must buy a vignette (rovinieta) upon entering Romania. They are sold at border stations or petrol pumps. In our experience, the quality of Romania’s interior roads pleasantly surprised us. In particular, the A1 motorway was a modern, broad, well-maintained European highway with several lanes. How Long It Takes: 3–4 hours from Calafat until you connect to the A1, then 5–6 hours along the A1 to the Nădlac border. Crossing Romania takes roughly 8–10 hours in total. Things to Watch Out For: You will find large supermarkets like Lidl and Kaufland along the route. These are great spots to take breaks and stock up on essentials. While LPG stations are common in Romania, some might be cash-only or require specific nozzle adapters. For details, check out: LPG in Europe Guide. Following Turkish semi-trucks can be a lifesaver here; truckers know the best, fastest, and smoothest routes. Online / In-Person: Rovinieta can be purchased online (roviniete.ro) or physically. Border procedures are in-person. Step 4: Hungary (Nădlac/Arad – Budapest – Hegyeshalom Border) # Where: Enter Hungary from Romania via the Nădlac border crossing and take the M43/M5 motorways toward Budapest. Then continue along the M1 motorway towards the Austrian border at Hegyeshalom. How: Hungary also operates an e-vignette (e-matrica) system. You can buy it at border offices, petrol stations, or online (nemzetiutdij.hu). Hungarian motorways are very smooth and fast. We stayed overnight in Budapest, which was a fantastic rest stop on this long journey. How Long It Takes: 2.5–3 hours from Nădlac to Budapest, and 1.5–2 hours from Budapest to Hegyeshalom. Total crossing through Hungary takes about 4–5 hours. Things to Watch Out For: Petrol stations and service rest areas are frequent across Hungary. Budapest is ideal for an overnight stop thanks to its historic atmosphere and affordable lodging options. Online / In-Person: The e-vignette is usually purchased online or registered digitally at gas stations. Border controls are done in-person. Step 5: Austria (Hegyeshalom – Vienna – Passau Border) # Where: Enter Austria via the Hegyeshalom border, take the A4 motorway to Vienna, and then continue along the A1 motorway toward the German border (Passau direction). How: A vignette (toll sticker) is mandatory in Austria as well. You can purchase it at the border, at the first fuel stops inside Austria, online (asfinag.at), or at automated kiosks. Short-term options (1-day, 10-day, 2-month) are available. Austrian motorways are top quality and very scenic. How Long It Takes: About 1 hour from Hegyeshalom to Vienna, and 2–3 hours from Vienna to the German border near Passau. Crossing Austria takes roughly 3–4 hours in total. Things to Watch Out For: Vignette enforcement cameras are everywhere and fines are hefty. Make sure to buy one and display it properly on the windshield if it’s a physical sticker. Comply strictly with speed limits and special tunnel regulations. Online / In-Person: Vignettes are purchased online (asfinag.at) or in physical form. Step 6: Germany (Passau – Munich) # Where: Enter Germany near Passau from Austria and follow the A3 and A92/A9 motorways to Munich. How: Motorways (Autobahn) in Germany are free of charge for passenger cars, so no vignette or road toll is required. Road quality is top-notch, and many stretches have no blanket speed limit (though the recommended speed, Richtgeschwindigkeit, is 130 km/h). How Long It Takes: 1.5–2 hours from Passau to Munich. Things to Watch Out For: Even though parts of the Autobahn lack a mandatory maximum speed, limits are strictly enforced during poor weather or in construction zones. Pay attention to dynamic overhead signs. Always use the left lane strictly for overtaking and yield promptly to faster traffic approaching from behind. Online / In-Person: The border crossing is generally seamless without systematic checks, though random border police spot checks can occur. Required Documents # Here is an overview of the essential documents you should have ready when traveling to Germany by car and getting settled:
Document Where to Obtain Description Valid Passports General Directorate of Civil Registration and Citizenship Affairs (Turkey) Passports for all travelers (including children) with at least 6 months of remaining validity. Schengen Visa German Embassy / Consulates (or visa application centres) A valid multiple-entry Schengen visa covering travel dates. Not required if you already hold a German residence permit. National ID Cards Civil Registration Directorate Can be presented alongside passports when exiting Turkey and at country borders. Turkish Driver’s License General Directorate of Security / Civil Registration Your valid Turkish driver’s license. You can use it in Germany for a limited period before needing a conversion. For more details: Driver’s License Conversion Process in Germany. International Driving Permit (Recommended) Touring and Automobile Club of Turkey (TTOK) Not strictly mandatory within Germany and the EU, but can help bridge potential language barriers during traffic stops. Vehicle Registration Document (Ruhsat) Traffic Registry / Notaries Proof of ownership of the vehicle. The original document must stay in the car. Green Card (Yeşil Sigorta) Your Insurance Company International certificate proving third-party motor liability coverage abroad. Can also be purchased at the border. Details: Green Card Insurance Guide. Vehicle Inspection Report (TÜVTÜRK) TÜVTÜRK Stations Valid inspection certificate proving roadworthiness. Power of Attorney (If Car Isn’t Registered to You) Notary Public If the vehicle is registered to someone else, you must carry a notarized power of attorney from the owner. Travel Health Insurance Insurance Companies Mandatory for Schengen visa applications and valid across all traveled countries. Multilingual Birth Certificates for Children Civil Registry Offices (Nüfus Müdürlüğü) Useful to prove parentage, especially when traveling with minors or handling specific administrative matters (like Bulgarian citizenship procedures). European Roadside Assistance (ADAC, etc.) Relevant auto clubs/providers Pre-arranged roadside assistance coverage in case of breakdowns abroad. Documents Requiring Translation, Apostille, or Legalization:
For the road trip itself, documents like passports, driver’s licenses, and car registration typically do not need translations or apostilles. However, if you plan to carry out official business on the road (like our citizenship application in Sofia), that specific document (such as a birth certificate) may need to be an international multilingual format or translated by a certified sworn translator. Always check requirements with the relevant authority in advance. Once you settle in Germany and convert your Turkish license at the Führerscheinstelle (driver’s licensing authority), you will need a sworn translation of your driving license. Costs and Travel Times # Driving from Istanbul to Munich can be more affordable than multiple flight tickets, but it comes with several visible and hidden expenses. Here is an estimated breakdown:
Official Road Tolls and Fees Table # Item Cost (EUR) (Estimated) Time Needed Bulgarian Vignette (weekend/weekly) ~10 EUR 10 mins (at the border) Romanian Rovinieta (7 days) ~10 EUR 10 mins (at the border) Hungarian E-vignette (10 days) ~16 EUR 5 mins (online / gas station) Austrian Vignette (10 days) ~10 EUR 5 mins (at the border) Calafat Bridge Toll 6–8 EUR 5 mins Green Card Insurance 75–150 EUR (annual) 10–15 mins (if bought at border) Total Estimated Mandatory Tolls & Fees ~127 – 204 EUR Other Expenses and Durations # Fuel (LPG / Petrol):
Distance: Approx. 1,500 km. Fuel Consumption: Average of 8 l/100 km (mixed LPG/petrol). Roughly 120 liters of total fuel. Fuel Prices: Across Europe, LPG averages around 0.70–1.00 EUR per liter, whereas petrol is roughly 1.50–1.90 EUR. Estimated Fuel Cost: For LPG: 120 l * 0.90 EUR = ~108 EUR For Petrol: 120 l * 1.70 EUR = ~204 EUR Note: LPG prices fluctuate significantly by country and even between individual stations. Romania and Bulgaria are comparatively cheaper, while Hungary and Austria lean pricier. You might also have to run on petrol briefly if an LPG adapter is missing. Accommodation:
We stayed one night in Budapest. Airbnb or hotel prices vary depending on your style. Estimated Cost: 60–120 EUR for one night. (We paid around 80 EUR.) Food and Drinks:
Snacks from supermarkets, petrol station coffees, and a few proper meals along the way. Estimated Cost: 50–100 EUR (depending on family size and preferences). Hidden and Unexpected Expenses:
Translations / Apostilles: If you need extra documents along the route (like our citizenship appointment in Bulgaria), sworn translation fees can run 20–50 EUR per document. Post / Shipping: In case you need to mail paperwork while traveling. Photos: Biometric passport photos if needed. Car Maintenance: Pre-trip servicing (oil, fluids, brake pads, tire check). While strictly speaking not a “travel cost,” it is essential for safety. Roadside Assistance: Annual membership for ADAC or a similar auto club (around 50–100 EUR). Kids’ Entertainment: Small toys, travel books, offline tablet downloads. Total Estimated Cost and Time:
Total Estimated Cost (Minimum): Around 350 – 550 EUR (depending on fuel type, accommodation, and food choices). Total Estimated Travel Time: Around 22–23 hours of non-stop driving. We completed this journey across 2 full days. Day 1: Istanbul into central Romania (around 12–14 hours on the road). Day 2: Romania to Munich (including the Budapest overnight, roughly 10–12 hours of driving). When traveling with small kids, stretching the itinerary over 3 days can offer a much calmer rhythm. Practical Tips # To help make this long drive from Istanbul to Munich as smooth and enjoyable as possible, here are the hands-on tips we picked up:
Check Green Card Scope and Plan Alternate Routes: Examine your Green Card policy thoroughly before leaving. Check which countries are included in coverage. In our case, our budget-friendly policy only covered EU member states, which forced us to take the Romania route rather than driving through Serbia. Always verify your territorial coverage well before departure. Learn more in our Green Card Insurance Guide. LPG Adapters and Refueling Strategy: If your car runs on LPG/autogas, prepare for varying filler nozzle adapters across Europe (Dish, ACME, Bajonet, Euronozzle). Our Honda Civic needed different connectors, and some rural stations lacked adapters to lend. Keep a personal set of universal brass adapters in your glove box and verify what standard each country uses ahead of time. Note that in some European countries, you have to pump LPG yourself. Our LPG in Europe Guide covers all of this in detail. The “Follow the Turkish Trucks” Tactic: Especially in unfamiliar territory like Romania, tailing Turkish-plated semi-trucks is a surprisingly reliable strategy. Long-haul truckers drive these corridors countless times a year and know the smoothest roads, speed trap locations, and safe rest stops. They often provide better real-time navigation than any GPS app. Night Driving with Small Kids: When traveling with little ones, night driving can be an absolute lifesaver. We set off right around our kids’ bedtime (20:00–21:00). While they slept soundly in the back, we covered the most demanding stretches quietly. When fatigue hits around 2:00 or 3:00 AM, pull into a large, well-lit service station, lock the doors, and nap in the car for 3–4 hours. Waking up refreshed lets you continue without ever disrupting the children’s sleep rhythms. Don’t Forget Vignettes and Verify Plate Numbers: Vignettes are mandatory on motorways across Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, and Austria. Buy them immediately after border posts or at the very first service area. If purchasing digital vignettes, double-check that your license plate number and country code are entered correctly. Driving without a vignette triggers steep automated fines. In Austria, ensure any physical toll sticker is placed correctly on the windshield. Smooth Border Crossings: Keep all passports, visas, vehicle registration papers, insurance cards, and driving licenses grouped in an easily accessible folder. Crossings between EU/Schengen borders (like Hungary to Austria) rarely involve full checks, but random spot checks are always possible. Tips for Settling in Germany: A few reminders for when you finally arrive: you can use your Turkish driving license for up to six months after registering your residence (Anmeldung), after which you must convert it to a German license. Check our guide on the Driver’s License Conversion Process in Germany. If you hold a Bulgarian license or are looking into EU driving privileges, read our post Can You Drive in Germany with a Bulgarian License?. Finally, securing long-term housing is another huge milestone—our Renting an Apartment in Germany Guide will walk you through that step. Our Personal Experience # Driving from Istanbul to Munich was an unforgettable bundle of memories from start to finish. To be completely honest, the prospect of tackling 1,500 km in our own car with two small kids (aged 1 and 5) felt quite intimidating at first. We repeatedly asked ourselves, “Wouldn’t flying just be easier?” But the mountain of luggage we needed to transport, paired with the sheer stress of managing toddlers through airports and luggage claims, pushed us toward this adventurous choice. Looking back, we are so glad we did it!
One of the most pleasant surprises was the quality of Romanian motorways. Setting off with typical Western European expectations, we worried Romania might consist entirely of bumpy village roads. Instead, the A1 motorway proved wide, impeccably maintained, fast, and on par with the German Autobahn. That stretch turned out to be one of the smoothest, most enjoyable parts of the entire trip.
Our night driving tactic worked wonders. Eating up miles while the kids slept meant their biological clocks stayed undisturbed, and we avoided hours of “Are we there yet, Daddy?” Pulling into a service station around 02:00 to sleep in the car might sound uncomfortable at first, but it was surprisingly restful. Because the kids were in deep sleep, these brief stops didn’t disrupt them in the slightest.
The camaraderie of Turkish truck drivers on the road gave us memories we still cherish. We saw so many Turkish license plates through Romania and Hungary that it felt like driving in a moving community. During a fuel stop, a brief chat over tea with a Turkish truck driver parked next to us boosted our spirits and provided great tips about road conditions ahead. That warm sense of solidarity on the long road to a new life really touched our hearts.
The hardest part was undoubtedly the mountainous, winding stretch between Sofia and Calafat in Bulgaria. Navigating narrow curves in the dead of night through patchy fog was truly draining. On our return trip, however, seeing active highway and tunnel construction gave us hope that this section will soon be far easier to navigate.
Our one-night stop in Budapest gave us the exact breathing room we needed halfway through. A quick glimpse of the city’s historic charm, sleeping in a real bed, and waking up refreshed confirmed that breaking up the trip was the right move. If your schedule allows, I wholeheartedly recommend an overnight stay in Budapest.
All in all, this road trip did more than show us the changing faces of Europe. It brought our family closer together, proved we could overcome unexpected hurdles, and made stepping into a brand-new life feel like a shared triumph. Far better than we could have imagined, that journey was the perfect prologue to our new beginning in Germany.
Frequently Asked Questions # Q: Why not take the route through Serbia? A: While Serbia looks shorter on paper, budget Green Card vehicle insurance purchased on the Bulgarian border often only covers EU member states. Since Serbia is outside the EU, driving through would require purchasing expensive supplemental border insurance or risking refusal at the checkpoint.
Q: Are roads in Romania actually good? A: Yes, particularly Romania’s modern A1 motorway, which is wide, fast, and very well maintained. While the mountainous Bulgarian segment between Sofia and Calafat can be demanding, Romanian motorways meet high European standards and offer a very smooth drive.
Q: Is sleeping at a petrol station with kids safe? A: Large, well-lit, 24-hour motorway service areas with regular truck parking are generally safe. Always lock your car doors and crack windows just slightly for ventilation without letting outside noise overwhelm you. Well-known chains like OMV, MOL, and Lukoil across Romania, Hungary, and Austria are reliable choices.
Q: Is an International Driving Permit mandatory? A: In Germany and across the EU, your standard Turkish driver’s license is recognized for short-term visits and during your first six months of official residency. An International Driving Permit is not legally mandatory, though some drivers carry one to simplify communication during routine roadside checks.
Q: Where do I buy the Austrian vignette, and what happens if I skip it? A: You can purchase the Austrian vignette at fuel stations near the Hungarian-Austrian border, at the first service plazas inside Austria, or online via asfinag.at. Motorway cameras strictly enforce tolls, and fines for driving without a vignette are steep (typically 120–300 EUR). Never risk driving without one.
Q: Are credit cards accepted everywhere along the route? A: Major fuel chains, supermarkets, and motorway service plazas accept international credit cards without issue. However, smaller rural shops, independent stations, or certain LPG refill points may only take local cash. Carrying a moderate amount of Euros in cash is strongly recommended.
Q: What safety precautions should I take before such a long road trip? A: Give your vehicle a thorough mechanical checkup before leaving (engine oil, coolant, brake pads, tire pressure, and tire tread depth). Keep an EU-compliant first aid kit, warning triangle, reflective safety vests for all passengers inside the cabin, and a spare tire. Signing up for international roadside assistance (like ADAC) provides invaluable peace of mind in the event of an unexpected breakdown.
summary: Overview # Hello fellow expats and friends preparing to take their first steps into Germany! During our adventure of building a new life in Germany, we set out on a long family journey packed with our belongings: driving from Istanbul to Munich. This post serves as a guide for anyone considering this exact experience—hitting the road with two small kids, an LPG-powered car, and countless bags. If you are torn between flying and driving, or looking for practical solutions while moving to Germany, this detailed story of our experience is just for you.

Expat Guides — Processes I Actually Went Through # There’s plenty of information online about moving to Germany — but most of it is either official source summaries or incomplete.
Coming from Turkey and having also obtained Bulgarian citizenship, I went through several of these processes from two different angles. The path for someone arriving with a Turkish licence is different from someone with an EU licence. The rental market treats foreigners differently depending on their paperwork. Knowing what to do when you’re fired versus not knowing makes a very real difference in the outcome.
These guides exist to close that gap.
Driving Licence # Driving Licence Renewal in Germany How long can you drive in Germany on a foreign licence? What documents are needed, which office handles it, how long does it take and what does it cost?
→ Driving Licence Renewal in Germany
Is a Bulgarian Licence Valid in Germany? How different is the process for an EU citizen? Turkish-to-Bulgarian licence conversion and what it means for driving in Germany.
→ Bulgarian Licence Valid in Germany?
Housing # Renting in Munich Munich is one of Europe’s most expensive rental markets. Where to look, which platforms work, how to apply as a foreigner, and when to give up and try something different.
→ Renting in Germany — Munich Guide
Employment Law # Getting Fired and Going to Labour Court Dismissal in Germany is not as straightforward as it might seem. What the labour court process looks like, how long it takes, and what I would do differently.
→ Getting Fired in Germany: Labour Court
Driving and Travel # LPG Road Trip Across Europe Adapter incompatibilities, rules that vary by country, where to find LPG fuel, and the Honda Civic LPG experience on European roads.
→ LPG in Europe — Practical Guide
Istanbul to Munich by Road The Romania route, overnight driving, crossing Bulgaria and Austria, and how to deal with truck traffic on the long haul.
→ Istanbul to Munich by Road
Green Card Insurance What to watch out for when buying Green Card insurance at the border, the 90-day rule, and how to save money without cutting corners.
→ Green Card Insurance Guide

Bu yazı, meslek seçimi ve kariyer planlama üzerine hazırladığım “Meslek Seçmeden Önce” serisinin bir bölümü. Serinin tüm bölümleri: Kariyer
Bir önceki bölümde, bir mesleği değerlendirirken o meslekte bir günün, bir haftanın, bir ayın nasıl geçtiğine bakmak gerektiğini söyledim. Burada kendi alanımdan, IT’den bir örnek vermek istiyorum.
Amacım, bu işlere yeni başlayacak ya da adım atmayı düşünen kişilerin konuları biraz gözünde canlandırabilmesi. Kendimi onların yerine koyduğumda, kullanılan ifadelerin bir kısmının ne anlama geldiğini bilmediğim için anlayamadığım pek çok konu oluyor. O yüzden terimleri de kısaca açıklamaya çalışacağım.
Tabii burada işi çok genel anlatıyorum. Bir şirketin bilgi işlem departmanından (IT departmanı) bahsediyorum. Daha büyük şirketlerde çok daha farklı ekipler olabiliyor: sadece mobil uygulama geliştiren bir ekip, web sitesini yazan ayrı bir ekip gibi. Ekipler şirketin büyüklüğüne ve departmanlarına göre değişiyor.
Talepler nasıl geliyor? # Bir firmada çalıştığını düşün. Diğer departmanlarda çalışan kullanıcılar taleplerini genelde belirli bir yazılım üzerinden iletir. Bunlara help desk ya da ticket sistemi denir: her talep bir “kayıt” olarak açılır ve takip edilir. Böyle bir yazılım yoksa çalışanlar mail atarak ya da başka yollarla IT personeline ulaşır ve isteklerini iletir. IT personeli de bu istekleri yerine getirir.
Asıl iş: sistemleri ayakta tutmak # Halihazırda çalışan bir sistem olduğunu varsayalım. Sistem derken bir firmayı ayakta tutan her şeyi kastediyorum: kamera altyapısı, ağ altyapısı, sunucular, yazılımlar, donanımlar. IT personeli bunların yaşamının devam etmesi için gerekli çalışmaları yapar:
Yeni bir çalışan geldiğinde onun için gerekli ayarlamalar yapılır, yeni bir mail hesabı açılır. Bir personel işten ayrıldığında mail hesabı, şifresi, kullanıcısı kapatılır. Şirkette yeni bir departman açıldığında bu departman için gerekli ayarlamalar yapılır. Şirketin kullandığı sistemler eskir ve yenilenmesi gerekir. Bunu eski bir iPhone 15’ten iPhone 16’ya geçmek gibi düşünebilirsin: sistemin yedeğini alıp yeni sistemde ayağa kaldırıyorsun. Tabii arada ufak farklar, bazen problemler olabilir. Bazen donanımsal problemler olur, cihaz çalışmaz. Ölçek farkı # Bu işe yeni başlayanlar için biraz ölçeklendirme yapayım. Evinde bir laptopun var ve belki yılda 3–5 defa bununla ilgili bir problem yaşıyorsun. Ama bir şirkette 500 çalışan, 500 laptop olduğunu ve her laptopun yılda üç defa arıza verdiğini düşün: yılda 1.500 arızan oluyor. Her gün mutlaka yapacak bir işin çıkıyor.
Üstelik teknoloji sürekli gelişiyor, yazılımlar ve işletim sistemleri sürekli güncelleniyor. Senin de bunlara ayak uydurman gerekiyor.
Günlük hayatta karşılaşılan sorunlar # Günlük hayatta daha çok gündelik problemler oluyor:
Yazıcıdan çıktı alamayan bir kullanıcı Bir yere mail atamayan bir kullanıcı Bir web sitesine erişemeyen bir kullanıcı Santral üzerinden belirli bir numarayı arayamayan bir kullanıcı Laptopu bozulan, klavyesi ya da mouse’u çalışmayan, kulaklığı ya da ses ayarları sorun çıkaran kullanıcılar Yani onlarca, yüzlerce çeşit, hem yazılımsal hem donanımsal problem olabiliyor ve bunların hepsinin bir şekilde giderilmesi gerekiyor.
Seviyeler: 1, 2 ve 3 # Şirketler genelde birinci, ikinci ve üçüncü seviye gibi bir seviyelendirme yapıyor:
1. seviye: Kariyerinin başında olan çalışanlardan daha temel, daha basit görevleri yerine getirmeleri bekleniyor. 2. seviye: Burada tecrübe edinip kendini geliştirenler işin daha tecrübe gerektiren kısmına geçiyor. 3. seviye: Çok tecrübeli çalışanlar. Belirli bir sistemin yenilenmesi gerekiyorsa bu sistemden beklentiler neler, hangi üreticiler bu gereksinimleri karşılayabilir, hangi özellikler olmalı ve olmamalı gibi mimari yaklaşımlar, tasarımlar ve planlamalar daha çok bu ekiplerin işi. Mesai dışı çalışma: sektörün gerçeği # Biz IT personelleri genelde mesai saatleri içinde büyük değişiklikler yapmıyoruz. 8–17 arası çalışırken daha çok gündelik, basit işleri yapıyoruz. Tüm kullanıcıları etkileyecek, tüm sistemin çalışmasını etkileyecek değişiklikleri genelde mesai sonrasında yapıyoruz.
O yüzden bu alanda mesai dışında çok fazla çalışma oluyor ve bu alanda çalışmak isteyenlerin buna mutlaka adapte olabilmesi gerekiyor. Birçok firma bu mesai dışı çalışmalar için ayrı bir ödeme yapmıyor. Bazı firmalar başka günlerde kullanabileceğin izin hakkı tanıyabiliyor, bazıları hiçbir hak tanımıyor. Çok nadiren de ekstra mesainin parasını veren firmalar var. Böyle bir firmada çalışıyorsan gerçekten şanslısın demektir. Sektörün gerçeği bu.
Birçok firma artık sistemlerine uzaktan erişim sağlayabildiği için mesai sonrası çalışmaların çoğunu uzaktan yapabiliyorsun. Ama uzak bağlantını da etkileyecek kritik çalışmalarda firmada kalıp işi yerinde yapman bekleniyor.
Her şey “acil” # Size iletilen istekler genelde hep acil olarak iletilir ve bu aciliyete uymak zorunda kalırsın. Maalesef birçok firmada belirli bir IT süreci ya da onay süreci olmadığı için size iletilen işi hemen, hızlıca yapman gerekiyor. Basit olanları gün içinde yapıp, sistemi etkileyecek acil işler için mesai sonrasında çalışıyorsun.
Toplantılar ve ekip çalışması # Gün içinde toplantıların oluyor. Bir ekip olarak çalışıldığı için ekipteki arkadaşların neler yaptığını, neler değiştirdiğini, hangi işlerle uğraştığını birbirine iletmesi gerekiyor. Bunun için günlük ve haftalık toplantılar oluyor. Şirkete ve departmana göre değişse de örneğin günlük 15–20 dakikalık kısa bir toplantıda herkes yaklaşık 2 dakikada ne yaptığını anlatıyor, sonra işine devam ediyorsun. Bazen bu toplantılar uzayıp işin detayına giriliyor.
Bir örnek: Yöneticin sana bir görev verdi ve bu görevi yapmak için farklı bir ekipteki bir arkadaşla çalışman gerekiyor. Hem senin hem onun uygun olduğu bir saat ayarlanıyor ve bu zaman aralığında birlikte çalışıp görevi tamamlıyorsunuz.
Bilgi işlem departmanında çalıştığın için genelde diğer departmanlarla da birlikte iş yapmak zorundasın. O yüzden “ben bilgi işlemde çalışıyorum, benim işim sadece sistemler” diye düşünme. Birçok insanla muhatap olup, birlikte toplantı yapıp, birlikte çalışma planlaman gerekiyor. Şirketler de ekiple iyi çalışan, iyi geçinen, farklı departmanlarla iyi çalışabilen kişileri tercih ediyor.

Türkiye’deki hayatından memnun değilsen ve yurt dışına, özellikle Almanya’ya taşınmayı düşünüyorsan, bu yazı tam sana göre.
Tek bir tavsiyem var: bugün başla. Yarın değil, “her şey hazır olunca” değil. Nedenini kendi deneyimimle anlatayım.
Neden bugün? # Çünkü bekleme süresi çok uzun. Bizim yaşadığımız:
İş arama vizesi: Başvurumu yaptım. Randevuya davet eden mail yaklaşık bir yıl sonra geldi: “Randevuya gelecekseniz aşağıdaki linke tıklayın.” Aile birleşimi: Daha sonra iDATA üzerinden aile birleşimi randevusu için de başvurdum. Eşime davet maili yaklaşık 9–10 ay sonra geldi. Yani başvurduğun gün ile konsolosluğa gittiğin gün arasında bir yıl olabilir. O bir yıl boşa geçmek zorunda değil; ama başvuruyu yapmazsan o süre hiç başlamıyor.
Benim hikâyem # Bizim taşınma yolumuz aslında farklı oldu: Bulgar vatandaşlığımızı kullanarak taşındık. Ama bu vatandaşlık sürecimiz on yıldan fazla sürdü. Ne zaman sonuçlanacağını, sonuçlanıp sonuçlanmayacağını bilmiyorduk. O yüzden buna çok güvenemedik.
2024’te vatandaşlık süreci yine uzayınca “herhalde olmayacak” deyip internette bir videodan gördüğüm iş arama vizesine başvurdum. Başvurudan birkaç ay sonra vatandaşlığım çıktı. Bir yıl sonra randevu daveti geldiğinde ben zaten başka bir yoldan taşınmıştım; linke tıklamadım, randevuya gitmedim.
Yani o başvuru benim B planımdı. Vatandaşlık çıkmasaydı, bekleme süresinin büyük kısmı çoktan geçmiş olacaktı.
Bugün yapabileceğin 3 şey # 1. Başvuru sürecini başlat # Almanya’da iş aramak için bugünkü yol Chancenkarte (Fırsat Kartı). Elinde iş teklifi olmadan, Almanya’ya gelip iş araman için bir yıla kadar oturum veriyor. Resmi bilgilere göre ana şartlar kabaca şöyle:
Almanya’da tam tanınan bir diploma ya da meslek eğitimi, ya da kendi ülkende tanınan bir diploma/meslek eğitimi + puan sistemiyle en az 6 puan (tanınırlık, deneyim, Almanca, İngilizce, yaş, eş gibi kriterlerden). İkinci yolda en az A1 Almanca ya da B2 İngilizce. Geçimini kanıtlamak: bloke hesapta ayda en az 1.091 euro (2026 tutarı). İş ararken haftada 20 saate kadar yarı zamanlı çalışabiliyorsun. Başvuru, Alman Dışişleri’nin online portalı (Auslandsportal) üzerinden yapılıyor. Türkiye’de ulusal vize randevuları ise iDATA üzerinden veriliyor. Şartlar değişebiliyor; başvurmadan önce aşağıdaki resmi kaynaklara mutlaka bak.
2. LinkedIn’de konumunu değiştir # Bu, çoğu kişinin atladığı ama çok önemli bir nokta. Ben de LinkedIn üzerinden işe alım yaptım. İlan açarken “Türkiye dışından gelen başvuruları kabul etme” gibi bir filtre seçtiğinizde, o konumun dışındaki adayların başvurusu direkt elenir; ilanı açan kişinin önüne bile düşmez. Almanya’daki bir şirket de “sadece Almanya’dan başvurular” dediğinde, konumu Türkiye olan adayı hiç görmez.
O yüzden Almanya’ya başvuruyorsan konumunu Almanya yap ve yaşamak istediğin şehri seç.
Hangi şehri seçeceğini bilmiyorsan benim yaptığımı yapabilirsin: Ben önce Berlin’i seçtim. Birkaç ay iş ilanlarını takip ettim, göz gezdirdim. Baktım ki benim alanımda en çok seçenek Frankfurt’ta. Sonra konumumu Frankfurt olarak değiştirdim.
Sektörler de şehirlere göre değişiyor: Frankfurt’ta finans ağırlıklı, Hamburg’da liman ve lojistik, Stuttgart ve Münih tarafında otomotiv. Kendi sektörünün nerede yoğunlaştığına bakarak seçim yapabilirsin.
3. Beklerken Almanca öğren # Bir yıl, Almancaya sıfırdan başlayıp temel seviyeye gelmek için yeterli bir süre. Hem Chancenkarte puanına katkısı var, hem de buraya geldiğinde gündelik hayatta ve iş görüşmelerinde çok işine yarıyor.
Almanca kelime çalışmak için biz de Memorlex‘i kurduk; oradan yararlanabilirsin. Dil konusundaki tavsiyelerimi de dil bilmek ile konuşabilmek yazısında anlattım.
Kısacası # Süreç uzun ve kolay değil. Bekleme süresini kontrol edemiyorsun ama ne zaman başladığını kontrol edebilirsin. Başvurunu bugün başlat, LinkedIn konumunu güncelle, Almancaya başla.
Almanya’da hayatın nasıl olduğunu merak ediyorsan Türkiye mi Almanya mı? serisine bakabilirsin.
Not: Bu yazı kendi deneyimimi anlatıyor; hukuki danışmanlık değildir. Şartlar ve süreler değişebilir, güncel bilgi için resmi kaynakları kontrol et.
Resmi kaynaklar:
Make it in Germany: Chancenkarte Alman temsilcilikleri Türkiye: Çalışma amaçlı vize ve Chancenkarte başvurusu Alman temsilcilikleri Türkiye: Randevu alma (iDATA)

Bu yazı, meslek seçimi ve kariyer planlama üzerine hazırladığım “Meslek Seçmeden Önce” serisinin bir bölümü. Serinin tüm bölümleri: Kariyer
Kendi profilini çıkardın ve aklına yatan birkaç meslek var. Şimdi bu meslekleri değerlendirmen gerekiyor. Ben dört kritere bakmayı öneriyorum.
1. Gelecekte ne kadar talep görecek? # Herkesin ilk baktığı şey bu ve haklı olarak. Bu meslek gelecekte ne olacak, bu alanda iş bulma olasılığın ne kadar? Bir mesleğin gelecekte ne kadar talep göreceğine dair internette tahminler, araştırmalar var. Bunları bulup değerlendirmek, kriterlerden biri olarak kullanmak gerekiyor.
2. Ne kadar para kazanacaksın? # İkinci kriter maaş. Bunun için genelde o meslekteki güncel ortalama maaşlara bakılabilir.
3. O meslekteki insanlar nasıl yaşıyor? # Bence en önemli noktalardan biri bu: bu mesleği yapan insanların hayatı genelde nasıl geçiyor?
Şöyle düşünmek gerekiyor: Bu insanlar sabah 8’den akşam 5’e mi çalışıyor, yoksa farklı saatlerde mi? Birkaç örnek vereyim:
Restoranlarda garsonlar ve şefler belki güne öğlen 12’de başlayıp akşam 8’e kadar çalışıyor. Masa başında çalışanlar genelde 8–17 arası çalışıyor. Güvenlik görevlileri gibi bazı meslekler ise vardiyayla çalışmak zorunda. Hangi saatlerde çalışacağın, hayatının geri kalanını da belirliyor.
4. Bir günü, bir haftası, bir ayı nasıl geçiyor? # Bir başka konu da şu: o meslekte günler, haftalar, aylar nasıl geçiyor? Örneğin bir IT personelinin bir günü nasıl geçiyor, bir haftası nasıl, bir ayı nasıl? Biraz bunlara odaklanmak gerekiyor. (Bu sorunun cevabını kendi mesleğimden bir örnekle, serinin bir sonraki bölümünde anlatacağım.)
Sıralama önemli # Burada benim düşüncem şu: İnsanlar genelde mesleklere bakıp “daha iyi para kazanıyor, daha çok talep görüyor” diye seçiyorlar. Bence bu yanlış bir yöntem.
Önce kendi isteklerini bilmen gerekiyor: Neyi seviyorsun, ne yapmaktan hoşlanıyorsun, zamanını nasıl geçirmek istiyorsun? Talep ve maaş önemli kriterler, ama bir mesleği bu gözle, yani kendi hayatına ne kattığı gözüyle değerlendirdiğinde anlam kazanıyorlar.
Serinin sonraki bölümü: Örnek: IT’de Çalışmak Gerçekte Nasıl Bir Şey?

Hafta sonları iki küçük oğlumuzla genelde bölgesel trenlerle günübirlik gezilere çıkıyoruz. Zamanla bir düzenimiz oluştu. Burada bebek arabasının altına neler koyduğumuzu ve nelere dikkat ettiğimizi anlatıyorum.
Su ve mama # Su: En az 2–3 tane 1,5 litrelik su. Suluk: Genelde tek suluk alıyoruz. Küçük oğlum abisi ne yapıyorsa onu yapıyor; tek sulukla idare ediyorlar. Mama: Termosta sıcak su, yanında iki kaşık kadar toz mama. Lazım olunca orada hazırlıyoruz. Meyve ve fırın ürünleri # Genelde muz, elma gibi iki çeşit meyve alıyoruz.
Gezi pazar günüyse cumartesiden marketlerin fırın kısmından alışveriş yapıyoruz: kruvasan, buğdaylı ve çekirdekli çeşit çeşit ekmek, simite benzeyen Brezel, donut tarzı ürünler. Her marketin kendine özgü ürünleri var. Tatlı tarafında elmalı turta ve pasta çok fazla, vişneli tart da var. Bebek arabasının altı böylece doluyor.
Yemek götürmek zor # Çocuklar küçük olduğu için sandviç, peynir, zeytin, domates gibi şeyler çok uygun olmuyor. Nadiren yemek götürüyoruz: bulgur pilavı, pilav, makarna gibi çocukların sevdiği şeyler. Ama taşıması sıkıntılı; havalar güzelken bozulma riski var. Kışın henüz denemedik.
Bir arkadaşımızın tavsiyesi var: ağzı geniş kamp termosları. 8–10 tane almışlar; ikisine çorba, ikisine yemek koyup parkta açıp yiyorlar. İki erkek çocukla evde vakit geçirmek zor olduğu için onlar da dışarıda böyle yaşıyor. Biz de yakında deneyeceğiz.
Neden bu kadar hazırlık? # Birincisi, bölgesel trenlerle gezdiğimiz için yolculuk yavaş ve uzun. Trende yiyip atıştırarak vakit geçiriyoruz. Tren çok doluysa zor oluyor; merkezi duraklardan sonra boşalınca rahatlıyoruz.
İkincisi, dışarıda yemek pahalı; bunu ayrı bir yazıda anlatacağım.
Yanımızdakiler yetmezse gittiğimiz şehirdeki marketlerden alışveriş yapıyoruz. Gittiğimiz yerde genelde müzeleri, kiliseleri, tarihi yapıları, meydanları geziyoruz. Çocuklar patates kızartması ya da dondurma görünce istiyor; onları da orada alıyoruz.
Pazar günü dikkat # Almanya’da pazar günü marketler (Kaufland vb.) kapalı; pazar açmak için özel izin gerekiyor. Restoranlar, paket servis yerleri ve dondurmacılar genelde açık. Pazar günü dondurmacılarda aşırı yoğunluk ve sıra oluyor.
Her yer kapalıyken kiosklardan ya da benzin istasyonlarından bir şeyler alabiliyorsun.

Green Insurance Guide: We Saved 75 Euros at the Border — Here Are All the Details # Overview # Hello LebenInsider readers! As Turks considering moving to Germany or already driving on German roads, one of the biggest transitions in our lives is undoubtedly the status of our vehicles and driver’s licenses. Coming to Germany by car from Turkey, especially if it’s your first time, is quite an adventure. One of the most critical starting points of this adventure is Green Insurance, also known as the International Motor Insurance Card. If you plan to come to Europe with your vehicle, it’s legally impossible to set off without this document. So, what is this insurance, why is it so important, and most importantly: how can you prevent unnecessary extra money from leaving your pocket?
Green Insurance is a mandatory type of insurance that covers material and bodily damages you might cause to a third party in a potential accident abroad with your vehicle. Your traffic insurance in Turkey is only valid within the borders of Turkey. Therefore, as soon as you enter European Union countries, you must have this internationally valid document. It is one of the first documents that will be requested during police checks, at border crossings, or in any accident situation. If you do not have it with you, you may face serious consequences such as high fines or your vehicle being banned from traffic. For this reason, it is vital that you thoroughly research this topic and make the right decision before setting off.
So, who is this article for? We prepared it for anyone planning to move to Germany with their car, those who want to use their current vehicle in Europe, frequent travelers to and from Turkey, or simply anyone who wants to clarify the unknowns about green insurance. As with every step taken while building a life in Germany, we want to guide you through this process with practical information, ways to save money, and “what happened to us.” Thanks to this guide, you can travel legally and protect your budget.
Step-by-Step Process # The green insurance acquisition process essentially proceeds through two main scenarios: getting it from Turkey or getting it from the Bulgarian border. Both scenarios have their own advantages, disadvantages, and points to consider.
Step 1: Needs Analysis and Route Planning # Before deciding where to get green insurance, you need to clarify your travel route in Europe. This will determine not only the insurance cost but also whether your journey will go smoothly.
Where: This step is essentially a mental planning step. Open maps, mark the countries you will visit. How: You can use applications like Google Maps, ViaMichelin for route planning. How Long Does It Take: While route planning varies according to personal preferences, it is useful to allocate a few hours for detailed work. Points to Consider: If your route passes through non-EU Western Balkan countries like Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, the cheap green insurance you get from the Bulgarian border will not be valid. Although these countries are included in the Green Card system, insurance policies purchased from Bulgaria usually only cover EU countries. If your route will only pass through EU countries (e.g., Romania, Hungary, Austria, Germany), the Bulgarian border option might be more advantageous for you. Step 2: Getting Green Insurance from Turkey (Alternative A) # If your route includes non-EU countries or if you want to complete all your documents before the journey, getting green insurance from Turkey is the safest option.
Where: From authorized branches of the Turkish Touring and Automobile Club (Turing) or from agents of most insurance companies. How: You need to apply in person with your vehicle’s registration and the driver’s ID card/passport. Some insurance agencies can also process remotely. How Long Does It Take: Your policy is usually issued and delivered on the same day. Waiting times may increase depending on the intensity. Points to Consider: Prices may vary depending on the insurance company and comprehensive insurance status. It will be beneficial to get price quotes from at least 2-3 different places. Be sure to check the scope of the policy and which countries it is valid in. Institution Names: Turkish Touring and Automobile Club (Turing): Google Maps link will be added here, example: Istanbul Branch Contracted Insurance Agencies (e.g., Axa Sigorta, Allianz Sigorta, etc.) Online, In-Person, or Appointment Required: Most agencies prefer in-person transactions. Although some large insurance companies or digital insurance platforms offer online application options, in-person transactions are generally more common for green insurance as document verification is usually required. An appointment is generally not necessary, but it might be wise to call ahead during busy periods (summer months). Step 3: Getting Green Insurance at the Bulgarian Border (Alternative B) # This is the most attractive option for cost-conscious travelers on an EU route.
Where: At Turkey-Bulgaria border crossings (like Kapıkule, Dereköy), in small insurance offices or “booths” located right next to the transit lane. How: You go directly to the office with your passport, vehicle registration, and Euros to complete the transaction. Language is usually not a big problem; staff who speak basic English or Turkish can be found. How Long Does It Take: It can vary between 5-30 minutes depending on the intensity. The queue at the border crossing also affects this time. Points to Consider: The most critical point: These insurance policies generally only cover European Union countries. When purchasing the policy, be sure to check which countries are on the validity list. They usually show a map or a list of countries. With this insurance, you cannot enter non-EU countries like Serbia. You usually pay in Euros, so having cash is beneficial. Institution Names: These are private insurance offices; you can think of them as “Bulgarian Border Insurance Offices” rather than a specific institutional name. It is difficult to provide a specific Google Maps link because they are scattered at various crossing points. Online, In-Person, or Appointment Required: Definitely in-person and no appointment required. Transactions are done by going directly to these offices serving at the border. Step 4: Policy Delivery and Check # No matter where you get your insurance, what you need to do after receiving your policy is important.
Where: At the place where you purchased the insurance, immediately upon delivery. How: Check the accuracy of the information written on the policy, such as the vehicle license plate, chassis number, driver information, and validity dates. Especially review the list of covered countries again. Make sure the policy is wet-signed or stamped. How Long Does It Take: 2-3 minutes. Points to Consider: Keep a physical copy in an easily accessible place in the vehicle (like the glove compartment). Also, keeping a digital copy (photo or PDF) on your phone would be good for any eventuality. Required Documents # The basic documents you need to have with you for green insurance acquisition are:
Document Where to Obtain Description Vehicle Registration (Certificate of Registration) By the vehicle owner Contains all basic vehicle information such as license plate, chassis number, make-model. This information will be entered into the insurance policy. Driver’s License By the driver Required for verification of driver’s identity and license information. Passport / ID Card By the driver Required for verification of driver’s personal identity information. Current Traffic Insurance Policy From your insurance company in Turkey Although not directly related to green insurance, it can serve as a reference for your current insurance information. It is generally not mandatory, but may be requested in some cases. Documents Requiring Translation, Apostille, Approval: The green insurance policy itself does not require any translation or apostille. The policy is already issued in international standards and in English. However, if, God forbid, an accident occurs, the authorities of the relevant country may request a sworn translation of your vehicle’s registration or driver’s license. Therefore, as a general precaution, it may be useful to carry English or German translations of your important vehicle documents. However, such a document is not requested at the time of green insurance purchase.
Costs and Durations # Green insurance costs and duration vary greatly, especially depending on where you purchase it. Here is a general table:
Official Fee Table # Transaction Cost (EUR) Average Duration (Days) Green Insurance from Turkey (15 Days) ~48-55 15 Green Insurance from Turkey (1 Month) ~60-70 30 Green Insurance from Turkey (3 Months / 90 Days) ~110-125 90 Green Insurance from Turkey (6 Months) ~160-185 180 Green Insurance at the Bulgarian Border (3 Months / 90 Days) ~45-50 90 Note: These prices are estimated values for 2026 and may vary periodically. It is recommended to get quotes from relevant institutions for the most up-to-date prices.
Hidden Costs # While there are no direct “hidden costs” in purchasing green insurance, some indirect expenses may arise:
Exchange Rate Difference: Exchange rate fluctuations when paying in TL in Turkey or bank commissions for Euro-based transactions made with a credit card. Postage/Shipping Fee: If your insurance policy will be sent to you by cargo. (Very rare, usually delivered by hand.) Photo/Photocopy: Small expenses for copying documents. Cash at the Border: Cash Euro payment is usually requested at the Bulgarian border. If you don’t have cash, you may have to pay currency exchange commissions at the border. Fuel and Time Cost: Especially journeys you make to get prices from different agencies in Turkey or waiting times at the border crossing. Total Estimated Cost and Duration # If you need 3 months of green insurance:
Turkey Route (Comprehensive): With a cost of approximately 110-125 Euros, you will have an insurance valid for 90 days in all countries included in the Green Card system. The transaction usually takes less than half an hour. Bulgarian Border Route (EU Limited): With a cost of approximately 45-50 Euros, you will have an insurance valid for 90 days only in EU countries. The transaction time can vary between 5-30 minutes depending on the intensity at the border crossing. The total duration depends on the length of your journey and your stops. However, you don’t need to allocate more than a few hours for the insurance process itself. Practical Tips # Plan Your Route Early: Your travel route directly affects where you will get green insurance and therefore how much you will pay. If you plan to pass through non-EU countries like Serbia, remember that you need to get comprehensive insurance from Turkey. If you will pass through Romania, the affordable option at the Bulgarian border becomes attractive. For detailed information on this: By Car from Istanbul to Munich | Romania Route, Night Travel, and Truck Tactics Check and Read Your Policy: When you receive your insurance policy, make sure the information on it (license plate, chassis, validity date) is correct and especially that the list indicating which countries are covered is clear. Especially if you are getting it from Bulgaria, ask exactly what the phrase “covers EU countries” means. Carry Cash Euros: Insurance offices at the Bulgarian border usually prefer cash Euro payments. Having enough cash Euros (around 45-50 Euros), including small change, will speed up the process and prevent exchange rate/commission losses. Digital and Physical Copies: Make sure you have both a physical copy of your green insurance policy in an easily accessible place (glove compartment) and a digital copy on your phone (photo or PDF). This way, you will have a backup copy in case of loss or emergency. 90-Day Rule and Driver’s License Relationship: Green insurance usually offers a validity period of 90 days. This period refers to the maximum time your vehicle can legally stay in the EU. However, remember that the validity period of your Turkish driver’s license in Germany is also 6 months from your date of entry into the country. You should simultaneously monitor your insurance period and your driver’s license validity period and plan accordingly, whichever expires first. Otherwise, you will be driving illegally. For more detailed information on this: Driver’s License Renewal Process in Germany | The Truth About Turkish & Bulgarian Licenses Common Mistakes: Setting off without insurance, thinking “it will be fine anyway”: Never do this! The penalties and risks are very high. Getting the policy without checking it: Errors in coverage or information can jeopardize your entire journey. Focusing only on the price: The cheapest is not always the best, especially if the coverage includes non-EU countries. Leaving it to the last minute: You may lose time due to unexpected situations such as border congestion or system failures. Notes for Non-German Speakers: You can usually communicate with basic English at border crossings or insurance offices. Important keywords: “Green Card,” “Insurance,” “90 days,” “EU countries.” Having a translation app on your phone can also be helpful. Contact Your Insurer in Turkey: You can contact your comprehensive or traffic insurance company in Turkey beforehand to get information about green insurance. They might offer you a special quote or suggest additional products like travel insurance. Our Experience # During our relocation to Munich by car, the issue of green insurance was one of the first “small but important” bureaucratic hurdles we encountered. When we got a quote from Turkey, we were faced with a figure of around 120 Euros for 3 months of insurance. As budget-conscious expats, counting every penny, this amount seemed a bit high to us.
Based on our research before setting off and advice from other expat friends, we decided to consider the option of getting insurance at the Bulgarian border. We would redirect our route through Romania and Hungary to Germany instead of Serbia, which was a logical decision for us despite urban legends about bad roads in Romania.
After crossing Kapıkule, we saw small insurance offices right next to the first customs point on the Bulgarian side, near the area where trucks wait. The officers inside understood basic Turkish. We handed over our vehicle registration and passport. When the officer said, “90 days, 45 Euros for European Union countries,” we couldn’t believe our ears at first. It was almost a third of the price in Turkey! We immediately paid in cash Euros and received our policy. It was indeed a policy with only EU countries marked. This way, we saved a full 75 Euros. This money covered a tank of fuel for our journey or a significant portion of our first grocery shopping in Germany.
This experience was one of the first lessons that taught us how important research and trying alternative ways are when facing many bureaucratic hurdles in Germany and Europe. The Romania route was much more enjoyable than we expected, and the roads were quite good. The 15-20 minutes we spent at the border saved us both money and a practical lesson. This experience also improved our ability to manage time well and prioritize during the process of settling in Germany. We also painfully learned that we need to consider the vehicle’s stay in Germany within the first 90 days and the 6-month validity of the Turkish driver’s license together. Fortunately, our return date coincided shortly before the driver’s license period expired, and we did not experience any problems. But this showed how important it is to consider these two rules simultaneously when planning.
Frequently Asked Questions # 1. What is Green Insurance and why is it mandatory? Green Insurance (Green Card) is an internationally valid liability insurance that covers material and bodily damages you might cause to a third party in an accident abroad with your vehicle. Since traffic insurance in Turkey is invalid abroad, it is mandatory to be able to drive legally and to be protected against potential risks.
2. What is the difference between green insurance purchased from Turkey and at the border? Green insurance purchased from Turkey is generally valid in all countries included in the Green Card system (EU and some non-EU countries). Insurance purchased from the Bulgarian border, however, usually only covers EU countries and is therefore more affordable.
3. Can I go to Europe without green insurance? No, you cannot legally. If you are found without green insurance at border crossings or during traffic controls, you may face serious penalties such as heavy fines or your vehicle being banned from traffic.
4. What does the 90-day rule mean? Green insurance is generally valid for 90 days. This means your vehicle can legally stay in EU countries for a maximum of 90 days. At the end of this period, you must remove the vehicle from the country or renew the insurance. This rule should be planned in conjunction with the 6-month validity period of your Turkish driver’s license in Germany.
5. If I pass through Serbia, will the cheap insurance I bought from Bulgaria be valid? No, it will not. The affordable green insurance purchased from the Bulgarian border usually does not cover Serbia, as Serbia is not an EU member. If you plan to pass through Serbia, you need to get comprehensive green insurance from Turkey.
6. I lost my green insurance policy, what should I do? If you have a digital copy of your policy, you can use that. Otherwise, you need to contact the institution that issued the insurance (Turkish Touring or the border office) to request a copy. If it was lost during travel, you may need to inquire if you can obtain a temporary document from the nearest insurance agency.
7. How does green insurance work in case of an accident? In case of an accident, you should first notify the traffic police of the relevant country and have the necessary reports drawn up. You can call the emergency hotline of the insurance company specified in your green insurance policy to request assistance. It is important to act according to the instructions in your policy and local laws.
8. Does green insurance cover my vehicle’s comprehensive insurance needs abroad? No, green insurance only covers damages to the third party. For damages that may occur to your own vehicle, you may need to get additional insurance such as international comprehensive insurance or travel comprehensive insurance.
9. I have settled in Germany, when should I change my vehicle’s license plate? After settling in Germany, you must change your vehicle’s license plate to a German plate as soon as possible. Like your Turkish driver’s license, your Turkish-plated vehicle also has a certain legal usage period in Germany (usually 6 months or 1 year). You should contact the KFZ-Zulassungsstelle (Vehicle Registration Office) before this period expires.
10. Is there a relationship between a Schengen visa and green insurance? There is no direct relationship. A Schengen visa concerns your personal entry permit to Europe, while green insurance concerns your vehicle’s legal presence in Europe. However, it is important that the visa and insurance periods match for a smooth journey. For the Schengen visa process: Schengen Visa Application Process (2026) | Cosmos, Appointments, and Real Experiences
summary: Green Insurance Guide: We Saved 75 Euros at the Border — Here Are All the Details # Overview # Hello LebenInsider readers! As Turks considering moving to Germany or already driving on German roads, one of the biggest transitions in our lives is undoubtedly the status of our vehicles and driver’s licenses. Coming to Germany by car from Turkey, especially if it’s your first time, is quite an adventure. One of the most critical starting points of this adventure is Green Insurance, also known as the International Motor Insurance Card. If you plan to come to Europe with your vehicle, it’s legally impossible to set off without this document. So, what is this insurance, why is it so important, and most importantly: how can you prevent unnecessary extra money from leaving your pocket?
title: Green Insurance Guide | Save 75 Euros at the Border and the 90-Day Rule (2026)

Bugün Avusturya sınırına kadar gittik. Amacımız büyük bir şehir gezmek değildi; dağları, yeşilliği görmek ve trenle güzel bir yolculuk yapmaktı.
Sabah: bisiklet, römork, bebek arabası # Sabah büyük oğlumun dil terapisi randevusu vardı. Çocuklarla oraya bisikletle gittik. Benim elektrikli bir bisikletim ve arkasında bir römork var; çocukları okula bununla götürüp getiriyorum, gezmeye de bununla gidiyoruz.
Bisikleti ve römorku Pasing’de kilitleyip bıraktım. Eşim evden bebek arabasını getirdi, Pasing’de buluştuk.
Pasing mi, Hauptbahnhof mu? # Pasing evimize daha yakın, genelde oradan biniyoruz. Ama bazı trenler iki saatte bir kalkıyor. Vaktimiz varsa Hauptbahnhof’a gidip trenin ilk kalktığı yerden biniyoruz; çok daha rahat oluyor. Özellikle Augsburg yönü çok yoğun: Pasing’de bindiğinde oturacak yer bulamıyorsun, bebek arabasını yerleştiremiyorsun.
RB6 ile dağlara doğru # Pasing’den Garmisch-Partenkirchen ve Mittenwald üzerinden Scharnitz’e giden bölgesel tren var (RB6, Werdenfelsbahn). Bugün metro, S-Bahn ve trenlerde neredeyse her yerde tadilat vardı; bir noktada trenden inip aktarma otobüsüyle (SEV, Schienenersatzverkehr) devam ettik.
Yol boyunca manzara çok güzel: yeşillik, dağ etekleri, küçük göller, küçük nehirler. Huzur veren bir yolculuk.
Scharnitz: sınırın hemen öbür tarafı # Scharnitz’te açıkçası yapılacak pek bir şey yok. Biz zaten sınırı geçip dağ eteklerinde trenle yolculuk yapmak için gelmiştik. İstasyonun karşısında restoran gibi bir yer var; onun otoparkında çocuklar koşup oynadı. Bir sonraki otobüse 30–45 dakika vardı. Çocuklara yanımızdaki yiyecekleri yedirdik, su içtik, oynadık, sonra Mittenwald’a giden aktarma otobüsüne bindik.
Bilet notu: Deutschlandticket Mittenwald’a kadar geçerli. Mittenwald–Scharnitz arası Avusturya’da kaldığı için o parça için ayrı bilet gerekiyor.
Mittenwald # Mittenwald’da istasyonda inip yakındaki teleferiğe (Karwendelbahn) ulaşmaya çalıştık. Burada Almanya’nın en yüksek ikinci teleferiği olduğu söyleniyor; Zugspitze’den sonra geliyor, üst istasyon 2.200 metrenin üzerinde.
Şehrin her tarafında kazı vardı, yollar kapalıydı, alternatif yollardan dolaştık. Mittenwald’ın renkli boyalı evleri ayrı bir konu; onu ayrıca anlatacağım.
Yürüyüşçüler, bisikletliler, kampçılar # Bu bölgede dikkatimi çeken şey insanların doğayla iç içe olması. Çok sayıda insan doğa yürüyüşü yapıyor, bisikletle geziyor. Bu yöne giden trenlerde kamp eşyalarıyla dağa çıkan insanlara denk geliyorsun. Bisikletliler trenle bu kasabalara gelip oradan dağlara tırmanıyor.
Garmisch-Partenkirchen ve çevresinde çok fazla kış sporları mağazası var. Kayak takımı, kışlık mont gibi şeyleri kiralayabiliyorsun. Bu sektör burada çok canlı: otellerde, konaklamada yoğun talep var; teleferikle yukarı çıkıp aşağı kaymak çok yaygın.
Kimin için uygun? # Büyük bir şehir gezisi bekliyorsan Scharnitz sana göre değil. Ama Münih’ten çıkıp birkaç saat trenle dağların arasından geçmek, çocuklarla sakin bir gün geçirmek istiyorsan güzel bir rota. Yanınıza yiyecek almayı unutmayın; çocuklarla günübirlik gezi için neler hazırladığımızı ayrı bir yazıda anlattım.
